final_proof:
We use the Dedekind-cut construction of the real numbers; this proves the result without assuming any equivalent completeness theorem. (If the real numbers are instead introduced axiomatically as a complete ordered field, the assertion is precisely the completeness axiom.)

Recall that a Dedekind cut is a subset A of Q satisfying the following conditions: A is nonempty and is not all of Q; if r is in A and q < r, then q is in A; and A has no greatest element. In this construction, the real numbers are the Dedekind cuts, and their order is inclusion: A <= B if and only if A is a subset of B.

Let S be a nonempty set of real numbers which is bounded above. Thus, regarded as a nonempty family of Dedekind cuts, S has an upper bound U: for every A in S, A is a subset of U. Define

    L = union over A in S of A.

We first verify that L is itself a Dedekind cut. Because S is nonempty, choose A_0 in S. Since A_0 is nonempty and A_0 is a subset of L, the set L is nonempty. Moreover, L is a subset of U. Since U is a proper subset of Q, L is also a proper subset of Q. If r is in L and q < r, then r belongs to some A in S; the downward-closed property of A gives q in A, and hence q in L. Finally, if r is in L, then r belongs to some A in S. Because A has no greatest element, there is a rational t in A with r < t. Then t is in L, so r is not a greatest element of L. Therefore L is a Dedekind cut and hence represents a real number.

For every A in S we have A contained in L, so L is an upper bound of S. Now let V be any upper bound of S. Then A is contained in V for every A in S. Taking the union over all A in S gives L contained in V. Thus L is no larger than every upper bound of S. Consequently L is the least upper bound of S, so sup S = L exists in R. This proves the least upper bound property.
